items.title: Nicole C. Mullen Gets Candid About Sin, Betrayal, and God
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Encouraging.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Singer Nicole C. Mullen is on a mission to inspire people to make “godly decisions.”

Mullen said her new book, “It’s Never Wrong to Do the Right Thing: Courageous Stories to Inspire Godly Decisions,” was written to inspire others to look to the Lord as they navigate their lives.

“I love it that it says over in Matthew 6:33, it gives us the formula,” she said. “It tells us to seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness — His right way of doing things, His right standing, and then He promises that everything else that we need, whether it’s relationships, finances, whether it’s health, whether it’s mental sanity … whatever it is that we need will be added.”

Mullen said her book intends to encourage people in this area, explaining how being candid and sharing her journey with sin and struggle is helpful to others. This meant opening up about domestic violence, betrayal, and other personal matters.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

“I know that even in my weakness, Christ is strong,” she said. “I say all the time, ‘Lord, I bring my weakness to the table,’ and sometimes it comes with embarrassing moments. Sometimes it comes with me not looking as good as I would want to look. But at the end of the day, He’s always the hero; He’s always the champion.”

Mullen said she shared some personal anecdotes and stories in the book for that very reason. The singer pointed back to Scripture, too, where some raw and candid stories often show people’s flaws.

“Even in the Scriptures, I find that there are no perfect people except one … and that’s Christ Himself,” she said. “Everybody else was messed up. Everybody else … just made horrible decisions and all kinds of things, but I find that, when they sought God — when they did it His way, He gave them success through it, even if it didn’t turn out the way they thought.”

With that in mind, Mullen said she brought together numerous stories showing this very dynamic in her book, “It’s Never Wrong to Do the Right Thing.”

“I wanted to pull out everyday people to show us that we don’t have to be famous to make the right decision and have great impact,” Mullen said. “We just have to be found faithful to do what God has called us to do in the moment, and, when we do that, and oftentimes it’s in scary situations — it’s in difficult times.”

When we’re faced with right or wrong, Mullen said God will show up and give us what we need.

“Even if we don’t see it in the moment, we can trust God to know that He’s working together for our good and the benefit of other people as well,” she said.

Ultimately, Mullen said Christians must show up and “seek first the Kingdom of God” in any and all seasons.

“The Bible speaks to everything,” she said. “Even though the cultures may have been different, human nature … still the same. We still face the same fears, the same temptations, the same desires, the same insecurities.”

Find out more about Mullen’s book, “It’s Never Wrong to Do the Right Thing.”

items.title: Where God Reigns
items.author: Marvin Williams
items.summary:
In 2018, a man checked into a room at New York hotel for a one-night stay. Remarkably, he used the room for five years without paying another cent—exploiting obscure rent laws to hold on to it. His refusal to leave, however, eventually led to potential prison time for him.
Like an unwelcome te
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

In 2018, a man checked into a room at New York hotel for a one-night stay. Remarkably, he used the room for five years without paying another cent—exploiting obscure rent laws to hold on to it. His refusal to leave, however, eventually led to potential prison time for him.

Like an unwelcome tenant who overstays, James warns us that the devil lingers in our lives when left unchecked. “Resist the devil,” James writes, “and he will flee from you” (4:7). The apostle emphasizes that our struggles often come from impure “desires” and “wrong motives” (vv. 1, 3)—things like pride, divided loyalties, and impure thoughts residing in our hearts. To counter such temptation, James offers two commands: “submit . . . to God” and “resist the devil” (v. 7). To submit means surrendering every part of our lives to God. Resisting the devil is equally active, requiring prayer, vigilance, and the wisdom of Scripture.

Like a landlord evicting an unlawful tenant, in God’s strength we can refuse to let the temptation of the devil overtake us. As we resist him, God promises victory as James asserts: “He will flee from you” (v. 7).

When we evict sin and the devil’s influence and “come near to God” (v. 8), we allow His peace, joy, and purpose to dwell more fully in us. The enemy can’t stay where God reigns!

items.title: Power of Consistent Prayer
items.author: Lisa M. Samra
items.summary:
Speaking to a group of young actors, Academy-Award-winning actor Denzel Washington encouraged them to begin each day with prayer, suggesting they “put your shoes way under the bed at night” to ensure they "gotta get on your knees in the morning.”
Developing a regular habit of praye
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Speaking to a group of young actors, Academy-Award-winning actor Denzel Washington encouraged them to begin each day with prayer, suggesting they “put your shoes way under the bed at night” to ensure they "gotta get on your knees in the morning.”

Developing a regular habit of prayer might take some thoughtful and even creative planning, but it’s a practice that has sustained God’s people throughout history—especially in difficult times. We see this in the life of Daniel, who was served in King Darius’ administration. He quickly distinguished himself as the top government advisor, which angered local officials. Out of jealously they plotted to oust the prophet, but they quickly realized the only charge that would stick was related to Daniel’s well-known habit of prayer. Even after the officials tricked the king into making it illegal for Daniel to pray, Daniel still “got down on his knees, and prayed . . . just as he had done before” (Daniel 6:10).

A consistent prayer life was essential for Daniel to experience God’s sustaining strength and peace (Psalm 29:11). It helped him to triumph over the forces seeking to destroy him. In the same way, establishing a regular time to meet with God in prayer and making it a daily priority can help cultivate our relationship with Him. During each difficulty we face, it’s His strength that will sustain us.

items.title: A Living Sacrifice
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, for this Twenty-second Sunday in Ordinary Time, I want to begin with our very brief second reading from Paul to the Romans.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, for this Twenty-second Sunday in Ordinary Time, I want to begin with our very brief second reading from Paul to the Romans. It opens, “I urge you, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice.” Here we see Christ’s cross and resurrection—the supreme sacrifice fulfilling all the offerings of the temple—extended to all the baptized. The Church is now the place where divinity and humanity are reconciled.

Daily Reading

First Reading
Jeremiah 20:7-9

O Lord, you have enticed me,
    and I was enticed;
you have overpowered me,
    and you have prevailed.
I have become a laughingstock all day long;
    everyone mocks me.
For whenever I speak, I must cry out,
    I must shout, “Violence and destruction!”
For the word of the Lord has become for me
    a reproach and derision all day long.
If I say, “I will not mention him,
    or speak any more in his name,”
then within me there is something like a burning fire
    shut up in my bones;
I am weary with holding it in,
    and I cannot.

Psalm
Psalm 63:2, 3-4, 5-6, 8-9

So I have looked upon you in the sanctuary,
    beholding your power and glory.
Because your steadfast love is better than life,
    my lips will praise you.
So I will bless you as long as I live;
    I will lift up my hands and call on your name.
My soul is satisfied as with a rich feast,
    and my mouth praises you with joyful lips
when I think of you on my bed,
    and meditate on you in the watches of the night;
for you have been my help,
    and in the shadow of your wings I sing for joy.
My soul clings to you;
    your right hand upholds me.
But those who seek to destroy my life
    shall go down into the depths of the earth.

Second Reading
Romans 12:1-2

I appeal to you therefore, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your minds, so that you may discern what is the will of God—what is good and acceptable and perfect.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 16:21-27

From that time on, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and undergo great suffering at the hands of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “God forbid it, Lord! This must never happen to you.” But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me; for you are setting your mind not on divine things but on human things.”

Then Jesus told his disciples, “If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me. For those who want to save their life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit them if they gain the whole world but forfeit their life? Or what will they give in return for their life?

“For the Son of Man is to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay everyone for what has been done.

items.title: ‘This Birth Season of Decease’: Joy, Loss, and the Immaculate Heart
items.author: Larisa Boulet
items.summary:
Larisa Boulet

How does one live under the weight of the birth-death paradox? How does the human heart experience these extremes all at once?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Larisa Boulet

On an ordinary Tuesday evening, I was walking through my apartment door when my mom called to tell me that my fifty-three-year-old dad had suddenly died from a heart attack. As my mom and I both wrestled to find words for the inexpressible, I stood in the entrance to the nursery for my unborn baby who would be thirty-eight weeks in just a handful of days. The sheer joy of my first year of marriage and my pure excitement over the birth of our first child gave way to shock and reeling emotion. Calvary had come to Bethlehem, and I didn’t know what to do. 

Through the generosity of a dear friend and the providence of God, my husband and I were able to drive from our home in Alabama to Indiana for my dad’s funeral, despite my imminent due date. It was just under a year since our wedding, and I genuinely would have preferred physical torture to processing down the same aisle my dad had walked me down—this time standing behind my husband as he helped to carry my dad’s coffin. But despite my own sadness, I could feel my precious, innocent baby kicking me throughout the funeral Mass. The sweetness of new life was here at the tomb, even though I didn’t know what to do. 

Eleven days after her grandfather’s death, on the Memorial of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, our beautiful daughter made her entrance into the world. She took her sweet time—labor started early Thursday morning and she was born at 2:10 am on Saturday—but it was the most peaceful, calm labor I could have asked for. Our nurse’s name was Mary Elizabeth, which I thought was such a sweet reminder of Mary’s visitation; I prayed with a small crucifix that my husband now blesses the baby with every night; and labor was long enough that my mom was able to make it in time to help us through the most difficult parts and to see the birth of her granddaughter. Looking down and seeing the little girl I had already come to know and love over the last nine months is a memory that will stay with me forever. Her name, Alethea Rose, signifies that Truth himself, Jesus Christ, rose from the falsehood of death and promises to bring all lovers of truth, like my dad, to paradise with him. 

The events of my dad’s passing and my daughter’s birth are inseparable in my mind: The grief wouldn’t be as terrible if he had gotten to meet her, and her birth wouldn’t have been as beautiful if he hadn’t been interceding for us in eternity (given his full-time ministry in the pro-life movement and his own vocation helping my mom give birth to five girls, I think he knew more than most that birth is a sacred event). Throughout this bleary-eyed experience of postpartum, I have wrestled with how to hold my greatest joy while simultaneously bearing my heaviest cross. 

T. S. Eliot gives some voice to my experience through his articulation of what Eliot scholars call the “birth-death paradox.” In “Journey of the Magi,” he writes,

were we led all that way for
Birth or Death? There was a Birth, certainly,
We had evidence and no doubt. I had seen birth and death,
But had thought they were different; this Birth was
Hard and bitter agony for us, like Death, our death.

And in “A Song for Simeon,” he writes,

Before the certain hour of maternal sorrow, 
Now at this birth season of decease, 
Let the Infant, the still unspeaking and unspoken Word, 
Grant Israel’s consolation 
To one who has eighty years and no tomorrow. 

Christ’s birth brought unspeakable joy, yes, but it also brought with it the demands of discipleship, the call to encounter healing from the birth pangs of original sin only through the deep suffering that comes with conformity to the crucified one. We enter the fullness of life not only through the metaphorical death of baptism but also through the very real death that each of us will one day face. And there’s no amount of poetry that can sugarcoat the reality that death was not a part of God’s plan and that the consequences of our sin and fallenness really, really hurt.

Order Your Set Today

Faith and hope are not electric blankets, as Flannery O’Connor would remind us. When I wake up in the middle of the night to nurse my baby, I fervently love her and the joy of motherhood while so heavily grieving my own daughterhood. I know that this experience isn’t unique to me: Lots of people become parents while grieving their own; laughter and joy even amidst the primal wounds of sin and death are just one of the many both/ands that we accept as Christians who “call this Friday good,” to quote Eliot once again. How does one live under the weight of the birth-death paradox? How does the human heart experience these extremes all at once?

Despite its overwhelm, this capacity of our hearts for the various extremities of love is a privilege of being a human person. It is a privilege and gift that the Church honors every August by dedicating the month to the Immaculate Heart of Mary. If there ever was a heart that knew rapturous joy, unimaginable sorrow, and how to hold these realities in tandem, it was Mary’s. 

I think our beautiful artistic devotions to the holy hearts of Jesus and Mary sometimes leave us desensitized to the fact that these are real human hearts beating in heaven for love of the Father and with unspeakable love for each one of us. Mary’s heart was not actually crowned in roses and displayed on the Holy Family’s wall as decor. It was a physical heart shaped like yours and mine. In the Judeo-Christian tradition, the heart represents the innermost chamber of the human person, the place of intellectual and emotional encounter with the Godhead who exceeds our loftiest thoughts and noblest feelings. There is no dichotomy between intellect and affectivity; rather, the person perceives the world with utmost integrity of body, mind, and soul—although Jesus’s and Mary’s hearts were the only ones to do so perfectly!

Luke’s Gospel repeatedly emphasizes the beauty of Mary’s heart and the riches therein. At the close of the Nativity narrative, we read, “But Mary kept all these things, pondering them in her heart”; again, after Jesus is lost and found in the temple, Luke tells us, “His mother kept all these things in her heart” (Luke 2:19, 51). With these words, Luke draws our attention to the vastness of Mary’s heart. She does not ponder or experience mere facets of the mysteries of Christ’s life; rather, she allows herself to hold “all these things.” 

That heart experienced the extremes of emotion with a beauty and poignancy that you and I can only imagine. My delight in my baby is only an inkling of the delight Mary experienced before her Son of God. Conversely, the sorrow I feel seeing my daughter in pain is nothing compared to the pain and tenderness Mary had for Jesus in all of his suffering, from his infant cries in Egypt to the totality of misery on Calvary.

Mary had a father whose death she would have mourned, as I do now. When I feel helpless before my mom’s loss of a spouse, I can recall that Mary lost Joseph and that she knows my mom’s pain and walks with her in a way that nobody else can. And before the brutal unfairness of my grandmother at her son’s burial, I can remember a far more unjust separation of mother and child at a tomb outside of Jerusalem.

Mary’s heart did not shy away from the extremes to which the Father called her. She held all that was said about her son, all of the love, all of the grief of understanding the words of the Old Testament prophets, of hearing Simeon’s prophecy, of losing her son for three days and knowing it was only a foretaste of the unfathomable loss she would suffer on Calvary. 

And eventually, her heart held all the souls of Christendom. The Church has perennially spoken of Christ’s death as the birth of the Church, a birth in which Mary, Mother of the Church, had no small participation. When we ordinary mothers bring a child into the world, our bodies are stretched to their limits, even torn apart, so that our hearts can welcome our son or daughter into the world. We don’t know the details of Mary giving birth to the Savior; we don’t know what stretching and aching, if any, took place throughout her pregnancy. But we do know that Mary’s fiat—first spoken in Nazareth but then echoed in every moment of her life, most palpably at the foot of the cross—stretched her heart so wide that it found room for billions of sinful children across the centuries.

It is the stretching of this heart—this immaculate, feminine, thoroughly human heart—that we commemorate every August. In honoring Mary’s heart, we learn to reverence our own hearts and the hearts of those we encounter. Mary’s heart is a promise to those of us who hold “all these things” of joy and grief far less gracefully than she, a testament that Gabriel’s words, “Do not be afraid,” apply not only to her but to the many whose own thoughts, loves, and heartaches mystically participate in the paschal mystery of her son. Her promise to Venerable Lúcia dos Santos at Fatima is her promise to each one of us in this vale of tears: “I will be with you always, and my Immaculate Heart will be your comfort and the way which will lead you to God.” Before the most tender places in our hearts, she knows what to do, even when we do not; she walks with us in the paradox of birth and death.
